title: Multi-Region Design: Active-Passive, Active-Active, and Conflicts
intro: Running in one region means a regional outage is your outage, and users far away wait longer. Running in several fixes both and creates the hardest problem in the field: the same data, written in two places, across a link slow enough to matter. The choice of model decides what you can promise. The shop wants to serve Europe and North America and survive losing either region.

steps.prompt: Measure why distance matters. From a host in Europe, time a request to the US region's health endpoint, https://us.shop.example.com/health: print the connect time and the total.
steps.explanation: 88 ms just to open the connection, and 291 ms in total with the TLS handshake and one request.
steps.why: A round trip across the Atlantic is about 80 to 100 ms and no engineering removes it. A page that makes ten sequential calls to a far region is a second slower. It also sets the price of consistency: a write that must be confirmed in both regions before returning costs at least one of those round trips every time.

steps.prompt:
In an active-passive design, one region takes all traffic and the other is a warm copy that takes over on failure. What's its main weakness?
  a) It's too consistent
  b) The passive region is rarely exercised: failover is a rare, manual, risky event, and the standby may not work when needed. Distant users are also always served from far away
  c) It costs nothing
  d) It can't use DNS
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
active-passive : one writer, simple data model, async copy -> RPO = replication lag, RTO = failover time
                 the standby is tested only if you test it (sre-tutorial-011)
steps.hint: What do you know about a system that has never taken traffic?
steps.explanation: Simple data, an untested standby, and no latency benefit.
steps.why: It's the right starting point for most systems because there's a single writer and so no conflicts. Its risk is that the second region is a hope until proven: capacity, configuration, and secrets drift. Regular failover drills, or sending a little real traffic through it, are what make it trustworthy.

steps.prompt:
In active-active, both regions accept writes. Two users, one per region, update the same customer's delivery address within the same second. What must the design decide?
  a) Nothing: databases handle it
  b) A conflict-resolution rule: both writes succeeded locally, so when they replicate, something must decide which survives or how they merge
  c) Which user to block
  d) To delete the customer
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
EU : address = 'Berlin'   at 12:00:00.410
US : address = 'Boston'   at 12:00:00.380

last-write-wins by timestamp : 'Berlin' survives, 'Boston' is silently lost (and clocks disagree)
per-field merge / CRDTs      : works for counters, sets; not for everything
avoid the conflict            : each record has a home region that owns its writes
steps.hint: Neither region knew about the other's write when it accepted its own.
steps.explanation: Concurrent writes to the same data need a rule, and every rule loses something.
steps.why: Last-write-wins is simple and discards data without telling anyone, and depends on clocks that aren't perfectly in sync. Merge-able data types work for some shapes. The most practical answer is to avoid conflicts by design: give each user or record a home region where its writes go, so both regions are active but no record has two writers.

steps.prompt:
Which data in the shop can safely be written in both regions with a simple merge, and which needs a single owner?
  a) Everything can be merged
  b) A shopping cart can be merged (take the union of items); an account balance or stock count can't be: two regions each selling 'the last item' oversells
  c) Nothing can be merged
  d) Only images
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
mergeable        : carts, likes, view counts, 'last seen'       (union / sum; brief disagreement is harmless)
needs one writer : balances, inventory, unique usernames, seats   (an invariant spans the regions)
steps.hint: Ask what goes wrong if both regions say yes at the same moment.
steps.explanation: Classify data by whether an invariant must hold globally.
steps.why: This is the design's central exercise. Where a wrong answer is cheap and repairable, accept eventual consistency and get low latency and full availability. Where a rule must never be broken, route those writes to one place or use a database that coordinates across regions and pay the latency. Most systems are a mix, decided per kind of data.

steps.prompt:
European customers' personal data must stay in the EU by law. How does that shape a multi-region design?
  a) It doesn't
  b) Data placement becomes a requirement: those users' records are stored and processed in the EU region, replication of them to other regions is restricted, and routing must send those users there
  c) Use a bigger US database
  d) Encrypt it and store it anywhere
Type the letter.
steps.fake_output:
users.home_region = 'eu'  -> rows live in the EU cluster only
global tables            : product catalogue, prices            (replicated everywhere)
regional tables          : customers, orders, payments          (pinned to the home region)
steps.hint: Not all data may be copied everywhere.
steps.explanation: Residency turns 'replicate everything everywhere' into a per-table decision.
steps.why: It lines up neatly with the home-region idea: the region that owns a user's writes also holds their data. The consequence is that a regional outage makes those users unavailable unless the law allows a copy elsewhere, a trade-off to settle with the legal team, not in an incident. Backups, logs, and analytics copies are covered by the same rule and are where it's usually broken.
